name: Francis Fukuyama
summary: Fukuyama is a liberal-democratic political scientist who argues that liberal democracy with market economies is the best-tested regime, but that it needs a capable, impartial state, social protection and a shared creedal national identity. He criticizes both neoliberal hostility to government and left identity politics and nationalist-populist identity politics, and supports regulating human biotechnology.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Writes that liberalism is compatible with wide state social protection, that universal access to health care does not make people lazy, and that the state is justified in supporting people hit by adverse circumstances (ch. 2); he does not set out a specific universal scheme.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Calls the insight into the superior efficiency of markets valid and credits privatization with beneficial effects in some sectors, while warning that markets need strong state rules and that finance cannot self-regulate (ch. 2).

public-ownership.rationale: Says Britain had no business owning steel or telecoms, which private operators ran more efficiently, though he also calls privatizing natural monopolies a travesty (ch. 2).

central-planning.rationale: States that socialist central planning was rightly discredited by the poor performance of communist economies (ch. 2).

regulate-corporations.rationale: Argues markets work only when states strictly enforce rules on transparency, contracts and ownership, and that deregulating finance was disastrous (ch. 2); he does not call for strict regulation of corporations in general.

social-market-economy.rationale: Writes that liberalism properly understood is compatible with a wide range of state social protections, that states must provide public goods markets will not, and that Scandinavia and the US are both liberal societies; sets social protection at a sustainable level (ch. 2, ch. 10).

free-trade.rationale: Says the basic doctrine is correct that lower trade barriers raise aggregate incomes, but that not every individual in every country benefits and low-skilled workers in rich countries lose, which contradicts "benefits everyone" (ch. 2).

no-central-bank.rationale: Argues the 2008 rescue by the Federal Reserve is the case for a large centralized state institution and that libertarians forgot the crises that hit the US before the Federal Reserve Act (ch. 2).

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Same passage (ch. 2): a central bank was necessary, and reliance on the gold standard without one meant periodic crises; he rejects replacing central banking with free-market money.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: Points to the gold-standard era without a central bank as a period of massive periodic financial crises (ch. 2); he does not address backing money with metals as such.

no-bailouts.rationale: Treats the Federal Reserve and central banks injecting liquidity to rescue the frozen payments system after Lehman as necessary (ch. 2).

corporate-influence.rationale: Writes that economic power has been able to buy influence in American politics and that interest groups exercise influence out of proportion to their place in society, mainly via legal donations and favours.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Writes that oligarchs convert economic resources into political power through lobbyists and media purchases, and that if inequality grows too extreme the political backlash against the system grows (ch. 2, ch. 10).

state-harmful.rationale: Calls hostility to government irrational and says liberal democracies need to acknowledge the need for government and a high-capacity state (ch. 2, ch. 10).

night-watchman-state.rationale: States that states are necessary to provide public goods markets will not, from public health to food safety, and that liberal states need strong government (ch. 2, ch. 10).

decide-locally.rationale: Principle in ch. 10: take federalism or subsidiarity seriously and devolve power to the lowest appropriate level, so democratic self-government takes precedence over uniformity, except where fundamental rights are at stake.

democracy-best.rationale: Defends liberal democracy as the regime to preserve and warns against leaders who use electoral mandates to attack liberal institutions (intro, ch. 10); he does not discuss the clause "even when voters choose badly".

consent-of-governed.rationale: Presents Locke's requirement that the state be constrained by the consent of the governed as part of the liberal tradition he defends (ch. 1).

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Defines liberalism as the rule of law, formal rules restricting even democratically legitimated executives, and defends it against Orbán- and Trump-style attacks on courts (intro, ch. 1).

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Defines liberalism as rules restricting the executive even when it is democratically elected, defends courts and independent institutions, and says voting rights are fundamental rights national government must defend (intro, ch. 1, ch. 10).

separated-powers.rationale: Words on both sides: he says the Constitution's checks and balances protect liberty, but that the American system has become a gridlocked vetocracy and that other democracies have stronger mechanisms for collective decisions.

direct-votes.rationale: Writes that ballot initiatives and similar participation reforms failed because publics cannot make large numbers of complex policy choices, which leaves activists in control (ch. on decay of institutions).

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Says shutting down disfavoured speech by governments, corporations or mobs is dangerous and will be wielded by others, accepting only narrow limits such as preventing immediate incitement (ch. 7).

individual-rights-only.rationale: Fourth principle in ch. 10: individual rights keep primacy over the rights of cultural groups; group recognition hardens differences.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: States that liberal societies assume equality of human dignity rooted in the ability to choose (ch. 10).

shared-human-nature.rationale: Argues human rights must ultimately rest on a concept of human nature and human ends, and defends a shared "Factor X" as the basis of equal dignity.

universal-morality.rationale: Argues rights are grounded in a common human nature and rejects the view that no shared essence exists, which would leave no ground to object to a genetic caste system.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Writes that liberal democracy has its own culture, which must be held in higher esteem than cultures rejecting democracy's values (ch. 11).

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Says social policies should aim at fluid categories like class, not fixed ones like race or ethnicity, and treats colour-blind meritocracy as a liberal standard (ch. 10).

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Says inequality in group outcomes is a by-product of many interacting factors, many beyond what policy can correct (ch. 10).

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Writes that "states' rights" was the banner for slavery and Jim Crow, and that the federal government rightly forced states to accept the legal equality of African Americans (ch. 10).

religious-nation.rationale: Calls for creedal national identities built on liberal-democratic ideas and rejects identities based on race, ethnicity or religion (ch. 11).

ethnic-nation.rationale: Argues national identity should be creedal, not ethnic, and criticizes jus sanguinis rules that privilege one ethnic group; he does not address demographic composition itself.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Says EU states with jus sanguinis citizenship should change to jus soli so as not to privilege one ethnic group (ch. 11).

allow-dual-citizenship.rationale: Calls dual citizenship a rather questionable practice if national identity is taken seriously, because of conflicting allegiances (ch. 11).

reduce-immigration.rationale: Says liberal democracies benefit greatly from immigration, faults the right for seeking to cut it off altogether, and says the focus should be on assimilation and numbers (ch. 11).

open-borders.rationale: Says democracies unquestionably have the right to control their borders and rejects a left view of virtually unlimited obligation to accept migrants (ch. 11).

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Calls for public policies to assimilate newcomers into a creedal national identity and for common schools; he does not demand that they give up their cultures.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Endorses stringent naturalization requirements such as the US ability to read, write and speak basic English, and criticizes multilingual programs that impede assimilation (ch. 11).

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Says noncitizens rightfully enjoy many legal rights and a range of state services such as education, and that only the vote is conveyed solely by citizenship (ch. 11).

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Says the vote is the major right conveyed solely by citizenship and that it is important to hold on to that distinction (ch. 11); he does not discuss local elections specifically.

patriotic-education.rationale: Calls for civics education to be revived in US schools and for common schools and a European identity inculcated by education (ch. 11).

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Words on both sides: says diversity benefits liberal democracies and well-assimilated immigrants bring healthy diversity, but that large and fast immigration weakens assimilation and support for welfare (ch. 11).

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Proposes that the EU create a single citizenship superseding national laws and shift powers from the Commission to the Parliament, while saying member states will resist (ch. 11).

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Writes that we do not want to replace national sovereignty with unaccountable international organizations and that the UN is not and will never become a legitimate seat of global governance.

force-without-un.rationale: Describes shifting the Kosovo intervention from a blocked Security Council to NATO as giving legitimacy the UN could not, and advocates forum shopping among institutions.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Advocates "realistic Wilsonianism": what goes on inside states is a proper object of US foreign policy and democracy promotion is hard but not impossible, to be done with prudence and humility.

democratic-peace.rationale: Argues liberal democracies replace the desire to be recognized as greater with a desire to be recognized as equal, and cites evidence that they do not fight one another (chs. on the "end of history").

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Treats NATO, the US-Japan treaty and similar US-built alliances as part of the order America should keep adapting, and says NATO could get a second wind.

evolved-behavioural-sex-differences.rationale: Argues evolutionary biology has shaped differing male and female minds and calls it implausible that all sex differences end with the body.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: States that men and women differ physiologically, genetically and neurologically, rejecting the view that all sex differences are socialized.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Rejects the view that male and female minds are essentially identical and that all sex differences are socialization, citing evolutionary adaptation.

human-enhancement.rationale: Proposes a regulatory line that directs biotechnology toward therapy and puts restrictions on enhancement, e.g. no making children smarter or taller, and calls for state regulation.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Accepts that conscious animals have a right not to suffer unduly, because they can anticipate suffering, while denying them rights that depend on human cognition.
